newsitem.title: USA: AWAY ON BUSINESS - Puddle jumpers upgrade.
newsitem.headline: AWAY ON BUSINESS - Puddle jumpers upgrade.

text.p: That puddle-jumping, open-air dash from the terminal to board a regional airline flight -- a common experience on trips to and from smaller cities -- is becoming a thing of the past at some airports.
At certain locations standard jetway bridges or other forms of covered walkways are or will soon be in use.

That's welcome news for business travelers and other frquent users of smaller airlines, which carried more than 57 million passengers last year, roughly one of every 11. It is also good news for disabled travelers.

The Regional Airline Association says the industry has launched a number of initiatives in search of ways to better protect passengers from the elements and insure their safety going to and from the planes.
One of the newest comes from American Eagle, which has found a way to use jetway bridges, the same ones that funnel passengers to and from big planes, for some smaller aircraft.

Simmons Airlines, the American Eagle carrier for a huge chunk of the nation's midsection, has already placed jetbridge adapters at 16 airports, based on a design idea from one of its employees in Champaign, Ill.
The adapter involved is essentially a gangplank-like device that connects the ramp to the plane's entry door. At the connecting point there is a canopy overhead, but the sides are open to the air.

In the next few months, the carrier will be installing 20 new bridges that are an improved version of the same idea in one American concourse at Chicago's O'Hare International Airport. The jetways are specially built to fit completely around the cabin doors of the aircraft.
Eagle boards 4,200 passengers a day at O'Hare.

At the moment, both versions of the jetway are designed for American Eagle's 64-seat Super ATR and 46-seat ATR-42 turboprops. The carrier said it is working with the jetway manufacturer to find an adaptation for the smaller SAAB 340B, which at the moment cannot use the bridges because of the location of the cabin door.

Ralph Richardi, president of Simmons, says "every place we've put it (the ramp adapter) the reaction has been the same -- people are very pleased with it. They like being off the ramp, like being out of the elements."

Walt Coleman, president of the Regional Airline Asslociation, said Comair, which is a Delta Airlines feeder, has installed a covered walkway in Cincinnati that leads directly to the plane, while other carriers have installed moveable covered walkways that can be pulled up to the aircraft.
While carriers continue to address the question, he said, there are many smaller one-level airports where jetways would not work, or where the volume of traffic does not warrant elaborate structures.

On another front, a recent Away on Business column (transmitted Sept. 26) that mentioned the "Pillow-To-Go" personal travel pillow listed an incorrect size for the item because of inprecise information received from the company. The pillow is 15 by 13 inches in size and about five and one-half inches thick (instead of 15 inches square and 13 inches thick).
